narrative:
The model predicts you have a 37% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you succeed.

The prediction is driven mainly by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence is your history of one past class failure. While most students who passed had zero previous failures, your experience with this setback pushed the model strongly toward expecting you to fail again.

Next, your weekly study time of 5-10 hours worked against you. Although this amount is not unusually low, the model sees it as less than what many successful students typically dedicate, nudging the prediction toward failure.

Finally, your clear desire to pursue higher education pulled the prediction in a more positive direction. This ambition is shared by every student who passed, and it helps offset some of the risk.

To improve, focus first on breaking the pattern of past failures by seeking help early in difficult subjects. Consider increasing your consistent study time beyond 5-10 hours each week, perhaps by creating a structured schedule. Build on your motivation for higher education by connecting daily effort to that long-term goal. Taking these steps now can reduce your risk and help you pass without needing further remedial requirements. (218 words)
